name: General Sherman Tree

location.address: Giant Forest, Sequoia National Park, Tulare County, California
location.neighbourhood: Giant Forest, on the Main Trail, about 0.5 miles from the Wolverton/Sherman Tree parking lot

access: Paid entry (Sequoia National Park entrance fee); a short, partly paved, downhill walk from the main parking lot (uphill on the return, or use the seasonal shuttle).
transport: No public transit; the nearest town is Three Rivers, CA, about 45 minutes' drive from the park entrance.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive and healthy as of 2024 remeasurement (National Champion Tree Program; NPS own page updated ongoing). By volume (roughly 1,487 cubic metres of trunk) it is the largest known living single-stem tree on Earth, which is the whole reason for its fame; height ~275 ft / 83.6 m is unremarkable for a sequoia, girth/volume is the record. Age is disputed between roughly 2,300-2,700 years (most cited) and as much as 3,200 years in some older estimates; both figures repeated here rather than picking a winner. Survived direct exposure to the 2021 KNP Complex Fire after park staff wrapped its base in protective foil; unharmed. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: YES, unambiguously - it is the most famous single tree in the US and the reason many visitors enter this part of the park. Two sources: Wikipedia (citing National Park Service and National Champion Tree Program data) and NPS's own page. girth_cm converted from cited circumference ~102.6 ft (1026.6 in) at base.

name: Colonel Armstrong

location.address: Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 17000 Armstrong Woods Road, Guerneville, California
location.neighbourhood: Pioneer Trail, about 0.5 miles from the reserve entrance

access: Paid entry (California State Parks day-use vehicle fee, about $10); flat, easy walk on the reserve's main loop trail, roughly 0.5 miles from the parking lot.
transport: No public transit; Guerneville town centre is about a 5-minute drive.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive as the reserve's oldest and most visited named tree; multiple 2020s tourism/park sources describe it as a current highlight of the reserve, and it survived the 2020 Walbridge Fire that threatened the reserve (firefighters worked to protect the grove). Named for Colonel James B. Armstrong (1824-1900), the lumberman who set aside this old-growth stand from logging in the 1870s-1880s; the man is dead, the tree named for him is not. Height ~300 ft, oldest tree in the grove (~1,400 years, some sources say up to 1,450). Clusters tightly with the Parson Jones Tree (usf_003, same reserve, ~500m away) and other named giants (Icicle Tree, Burbank Circle) on the same short loop, an easy walkable pair/cluster. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: borderline yes - it's the marquee named tree of a reserve people do travel specifically to see, though the reserve/grove as a whole is arguably the draw more than this one trunk. Coordinates from a geotagged 2023/2024 photograph of the specific named tree (Sarah Stierch, Wikimedia Commons), cross-checked against the reserve's own trail description (0.5 mi from entrance).

name: Davie Poplar

location.address: McCorkle Place, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.neighbourhood: McCorkle Place, the university's oldest quad, on public campus grounds

access: Free, open campus green space, no restrictions on approach.
transport: No public transit needed; on UNC's central Chapel Hill campus, walkable from downtown Chapel Hill.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive and standing as of 2025-2026 coverage (Daily Tar Heel, September 2025, on the 20th anniversary of a seed-distribution event; UNC's own founding-day traditions continue to reference the living tree). Named for General William R. Davie, credited as UNC's founder; campus legend holds the university was sited where he napped under this poplar in 1792, a legend rather than a documented fact and should be told as one. More than 100 ft tall (~30.5 m), more than 16 ft in circumference (~488 cm girth, converted from circumference), age estimated 300-375 years by UNC's own sources (basis not stated as growth-rate or ring count, treated as a vague-but-real estimate). IMPORTANT: this is ONE of three related plantings on campus - Davie Poplar (the original, this entry), Davie Poplar Jr. (a rooted layer/offshoot planted nearby decades ago) and Davie Poplar III (a more recent propagation) are separate trees; only the original is delivered here, the other two are leads for a future pass if UNC's campus cluster is ever worked up. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: modest yes for UNC alumni/campus history, no for a general visitor with no UNC connection; it works as a stop within a Chapel Hill cluster rather than a solo destination. location_precision set approximate: batch coordinate places it plausibly in McCorkle Place but is not confirmed against a tree-level source (no geotagged photo or campus map fetched this pass); a future pass should confirm against UNC's own campus map.

name: Doerner Fir

location.address: BLM land off Upper East Fork Brummit Road, Coos County, Oregon, west of Roseburg
location.neighbourhood: Doerner Fir Trailhead, reached via a mostly-paved BLM forest road with a final 4.5 miles of gravel

access: Free, on BLM public land; short, well-marked trail from a dedicated trailhead parking lot. Access road is remote (about an hour of driving from Roseburg on paved and then gravel BLM roads) and not maintained in winter.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Roseburg, OR, about an hour's drive.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive as recently as August 2025 (Smithsonian Magazine, Herald and News), which is when a mysterious multi-day fire damaged it; firefighters extinguished the blaze and the tree survived, though it lost roughly 50 feet off its top and with it its long-standing record as the world's tallest known Douglas fir. Previously measured at 325.8 ft (99.3 m), among the tallest non-redwood trees on Earth; current post-fire height not yet re-surveyed as of this pass, so height_m given (84m/~275ft) is an approximate post-loss figure from press coverage and should be re-verified once an official remeasurement exists. Formerly known as the Brummit Fir, renamed for a Douglas County commissioner. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes historically, as the record-holder with its own dedicated trailhead and trail register; the 2025 fire damage may have reduced that draw and should be reflected honestly in any story (a scarred giant that survived, rather than an unmarked record-holder). Two sources: Wikipedia and Smithsonian Magazine's contemporary fire coverage.

name: The Kalaloch Redcedar

location.address: Olympic National Park, off US Highway 101 between Ruby Beach and Kalaloch, Washington
location.neighbourhood: Kalaloch Big Cedar Nature Trail, a short flat walk from a signed roadside parking area

access: Free (within Olympic National Park); short, flat, well-marked trail a few hundred feet from a roadside parking pull-off on Highway 101. The access road has potholes but is passable by any vehicle.
transport: No public transit; nearest services are at Kalaloch Lodge, a few miles south.
verify_notes: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: on 8 March 2014 a coastal storm split this tree in two; roughly half of the trunk and crown fell, the other half remains standing. Multiple sources (KNKX, KOMO, Peninsula Daily News) describe it as still alive after the storm but now in slow decline. A May 2025 Washington Trails Association trip report and the WTA's own current hike page both treat the tree as an existing, visitable stop, with the WTA page carrying a standing caution to visitors about the 2014 damage and to heed on-site signage, which reads as current rather than historical guidance. So: alive as of the most recent (2025) trip report evidence, but visibly storm-damaged and past its former glory as one of the world's largest western redcedars (was cited at 19.8 ft / ~6m diameter, ~175 ft tall before the storm; girth_cm/height_m above are the pre-2014 record figures and should be captioned as such, not as current dimensions - no post-storm remeasurement was found this pass). Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes historically as a former champion tree with its own short nature trail; still a genuine draw for redwood/cedar enthusiasts even damaged, and honesty about the storm damage is itself part of the story. Two sources used: WTA (current) and KNKX (2014 storm reporting).

name: Lover's Oak

location.address: Intersection of Albany Street and Prince Street, Brunswick Old Town Historic District, Brunswick, Georgia
location.neighbourhood: Standing in the middle of Albany Street, just south of Prince Street, in the historic downtown

access: Free, on a public street in downtown Brunswick, visible and reachable at any time.
transport: No public transit needed; in central Brunswick, GA, walkable from downtown.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive, most recent dated photo evidence 2020; the city of Brunswick's own community page treats it as a current landmark and it remains a listed stop on local historic-district material. Unusual for standing IN the middle of a public street, which the road was built around rather than through. In 2015 a semi-truck crashed into the tree and removed one of its ten main limbs; it recovered and continues to stand. Age given as ~900 years / 12th century per Wikipedia and city sources, without a stated growth-rate or ring-count basis (a vague-source estimate, repeated as given rather than sharpened). Trunk diameter cited as 13 ft (4.0m), an unusually large figure for a live oak; flagged as worth a sanity check by a future pass since most record live oaks run smaller, though large old live oaks with heavy buttressing can measure wide at the base. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: no on its own - it's a beloved, unusual local landmark (a tree the town literally built its streets around) rather than a destination people cross the country for, but a strong stop for anyone already in coastal Georgia. Belongs to Brunswick, GA, which is not one of our currently published US cities and is roughly 75 miles / well over an hour from Savannah, so it does not qualify as a Savannah day-trip under the 30-minute rule; it stands as its own place.

name: El Palo Alto

location.address: El Palo Alto Park, on the banks of San Francisquito Creek near Alma Street, Palo Alto, California
location.neighbourhood: El Palo Alto Park, next to the Caltrain tracks where they cross Alma Street

access: Free, public park, visible and reachable at any time.
transport: Adjacent to the Palo Alto Caltrain corridor; walkable from downtown Palo Alto and University Ave Caltrain station.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive as of a March 2025 in-depth arborist/radar assessment (donated work by Arborist OnSite), which found some decay and a dead top but healthy buttress roots; actively monitored (ground-penetrating radar, air-spade root excavation, drone crown monitoring, a prism tracking movement). The namesake tree of the City of Palo Alto (Spanish for 'tall stick'); associated with a Spanish expedition campsite in 1769/1774-76 and appears on the city seal. Height has declined sharply from a measured 162 ft in 1930/1814-era surveys to about 110 ft today, attributed to a lowered water table between 1865 and 1955 killing the crown progressively; this is a genuine long-term decline story, not damage to hide. Diameter cited as 90 inches (~2.3m), girth_cm converted via circumference times pi. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: no for most visitors, but it is a genuine civic/historic landmark actively preserved at real cost by the city, Stanford and local arborists, worth including with that context rather than as a simple 'big tree' stop. Two sources: Wikipedia and the Garden Club of Palo Alto's own detailed history PDF.

name: Octopus Tree

location.address: Cape Meares State Scenic Viewpoint, near Cape Meares Lighthouse, Tillamook County, Oregon
location.neighbourhood: a short walk from the Cape Meares Lighthouse parking area

access: Free, Oregon State Parks scenic viewpoint; short, easy, well-marked walk from the lighthouse parking area.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Tillamook, OR, about a 20 to 25 minute drive.
verify_notes: Alive check: confirmed alive per Wikipedia (page last substantively updated July 2026), and a current, actively promoted stop in Oregon State Parks and Tillamook-area tourism material. Also called the Candelabra Tree, Council Tree or Monstrosity Tree. Unique form: no central trunk, instead six large candelabra-style limbs splay horizontally up to 16 ft from a roughly 50-ft-wide base before turning vertical; circumference over 46 ft (girth_cm converted from that figure). Local tradition (debated, not confirmed) holds Native Americans trained the young tree into this shape, possibly to cradle canoes in burial ritual; told here as tradition/debate, not fact. Designated an Oregon Heritage Tree. CORRECTION TO BATCH DATA: the coordinates supplied in the batch file (45.8922, -123.961601) are wrong, roughly 45 km north of the real site near Nehalem/Manzanita rather than Cape Meares; the coordinates above are Wikipedia's own sourced figure and match Cape Meares Lighthouse's known location, cross-checked against the park's own address. Would somebody travel specifically for this tree: yes - it is one of the most photographed and searched-for individual trees on the Oregon coast and a named reason people stop at Cape Meares.

name: Pando
age_estimate: estimated thousands of years (a single precise figure is disputed)

location.address: Old Spanish Trailhead, Highway 25 (Fishlake Scenic Byway), Fishlake National Forest, near Fish Lake, Utah
location.neighbourhood: the Old Spanish Trailhead parking area, where the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail runs a spur directly through the Pando clone

access: Free, US Forest Service land, no permit needed; a flat, easy 1.4-mile out-and-back trail from the Old Spanish Trailhead walks directly through the clone, and a further overlook is reachable via the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail off Forest Road 046N.
transport: No public transit; nearest town is Richfield, UT, about 25 minutes' drive.
verify_notes: NOT A SINGLE TRUNK: Pando is a single clonal organism, one root system, expressed as roughly 40,000 individual quaking aspen stems (trunks) spread across about 106 acres. This must be told honestly as an ensemble/organism, never as 'a tree' with one trunk in any photo. Judged against the collectible-point rule: there IS one obvious, signed, publicly reachable place to stand and experience it, the Old Spanish Trailhead, from which the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail runs a spur directly into the grove, so it passes and is delivered, with the pin at the trailhead/entry point rather than at any single stem. Age is genuinely disputed and not narrowed here: widely popularized as roughly 80,000 years based on a growth-rate estimate that is contested by other researchers who argue for a range from several hundred to about 14,000 years; conservation.org's own 2024 piece ('Methuselah: Still the world's oldest tree?') discusses this dispute directly. Recorded as unresolved rather than picking a number, per the rule against sharpening a vague/disputed figure. Alive check: unambiguously alive and an active subject of ongoing US Forest Service and conservation research and visitor programming as of 2025-2026 sources (Forest Service's own current recreation page, Friends of Pando). Some researchers report parts of the clone are struggling to regenerate due to deer and cattle browsing, which is a genuine conservation story worth telling honestly rather than a death signal for the organism as a whole. Would somebody travel specifically for this: yes - it is described as the world's most massive known living organism and draws dedicated visitors on that basis alone, distinct from the general beauty of Fish Lake. location_precision set approximate because the pin marks the trailhead/entry rather than a specific stem or the clone's true geographic centre, which is inherent to what this entry is.
